summary: Describes the technical procedures for remote printing in the TPC.INT subdomain, using Internet mail to reach printers connected to the telephone network. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 9121.

plainLanguage.summary: You send a document by email, and a helper machine near the receiver prints it on paper. This memo explains the steps.

questions: how remote printing over email worked
how did tpc.int remote printing work
subtitle: Using email to send documents for remote printing via facsimile machines.

tldr.problem: Before the Internet connected most printers, some documents needed to be printed at remote locations connected via telephone networks, and email was an available universal transport.
tldr.mechanism: Remote printing uses email to send documents to a server identified by a reversed telephone number as a domain name. The server receives the message, generates a cover sheet, and sends the document to a facsimile device at the specified telephone number.
tldr.outcome: The system was an experimental proof-of-concept that bridged email and facsimile networks, working in the early 1990s when fax was common but direct email-to-fax integration was not. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 9121.

today: RFC 1528 is now Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 9121. It was an experimental protocol that bridged email and facsimile networks in the early 1990s when fax machines were common but Internet-enabled printers were not yet widespread. The technique of encoding phone numbers in domain names was clever but never saw widespread adoption as direct IP-connected printers and modern cloud printing services became available.

sections.title: Remote Printing Over Email
sections.content:
This RFC defines a method for using Internet email to send documents to be printed at remote locations via facsimile (fax) devices. A user constructs an email message containing a document and sends it to a special address encoding a telephone number. A remote printing server receives the message, prepares a cover sheet with originator and recipient information, and submits the document to a G3-facsimile device connected to the telephone network.

The system works for various document types: plain text, PostScript, TIFF images, and MIME multipart messages. Support for recursive processing allows complex document structures to be printed with multiple pages as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: You email your document to a specially formatted address that contains a phone number. A server reads the email, makes a nice cover sheet, and dials up a fax machine to send it.

sections.title: Addressing Scheme
sections.content:
Remote printers are identified by their telephone numbers using the TPC.INT domain (Telecommunications). A telephone number like +1 415 968 2510 is reversed into domain labels: 0.1.5.2.8.6.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int. The local part of the address is remote-printer, with an optional opaque string for recipient identification.

An example address: remote-printer.John_Smith/Room_201@0.1.5.2.8.6.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int. Underscores in the opaque string are interpreted as spaces, and forward slashes as line breaks, so the recipient line on the cover sheet reads: 'To: John Smith / Room 201'.
sections.plainLanguage: The address uses the phone number backward as the domain, like reversing digits to get a unique name. You can add a person's name and room number to be printed on the cover sheet.

sections.title: Message Structure and Content Types
sections.content:
Messages with an explicit recipient identifier in the address must contain only the document content (text/plain, message/rfc822, application/postscript, image/tiff, or multipart). Messages without recipient identification use multipart/mixed with two parts: the first a application/remote-printing content-type containing originator and recipient information, and the second the actual document to print.

For multipart/mixed or multipart/digest, each subordinate part starts on a new page. With multipart/parallel, parts start on the same page if possible. PostScript content should be evaluated in a safe execution environment. Message content is returned to the originator indicating success or failure after the server attempts to reach the fax device.
sections.plainLanguage: You can either put recipient info in the email address (simple) or attach a cover-sheet file describing sender and receiver (detailed). The document can be text, images, or PostScript programs that draw pages.

sections.title: Cover Sheet Generation
sections.content:
The cover sheet typically contains three sections: originator information (extracted from the email's From header and any provided fields like Organization, Address, Telephone), recipient information (either from the address's opaque string or the explicit cover-sheet content-type), and optional information provided by the remote printer server.

When the recipient identifier is embedded in the address, a server that receives remote-printer.Arlington_Hewes/Room_403@0.1.5.2.8.6.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int interprets underscores as spaces and slashes as line breaks, producing: 'To: Arlington Hewes / Room 403'. Escaped characters allow literal underscores and slashes in the opaque string.
sections.plainLanguage: The cover sheet has a 'To:' section with the recipient (from the email address), a 'From:' section with the sender (from email headers), and any notes the server adds.

data.title: Example address construction
data.code:
Telephone: +1 415 968 2510

Reversed:  0.1.5.2.8.6.9.5.1.4.1

Full address: remote-printer@0.1.5.2.8.6.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int

With recipient: remote-printer.John_Smith/Room_201@0.1.5.2.8.6.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int
